matter-of-fact way of speaking that brings to mind a crushed peppercorn crisp.

released in Spain in 2022. Despite traditionally being less adventurous with crisps, Spanish
appetites have changed recently thanks to younger generations being exposed to different
crisps on their travels (and on the internet). So, Clifford collaborated with a TV chef to
recreate some traditional dishes. “I went to work with Quique Dacosta in his restaurant in
Spain. He showed me how he made this dish,” he says. The peppers are fried in charcoal-
infused oil to give them a smoky flavour. The sharpness of the pepper cuts through in the real
dish and the roasted wood-fired pepper with olive oil and garlic crisps.

launched in Pakistan in 2007, the team researched the country’s “culinary worldview”. “What

all flavours have the right spices that go with them,” Wade says. A tomato crisp wouldn’t taste

spices”. The company is evasive over email when asked what these spices are, but there are
clues on its packets. Swiss Grilled Cheese Lay’s available in Pakistan, for example, have
peppercorns and chilli pictured on the front. Spanish Tomato Tango Lay’s in India have
pictures of chilli oil and cinnamon sticks. Even when customers crave a taste of the world,
crisps are catered to local appetites.

mouth stuffed full of pepper in Clifford’s kitchen, I ask: “But how do you do it? How do you
turn this dish into a powder?” That’s when I discover that they don’t. “We partner up with

IV.	I first saw Hundreds Hall when I was ten years old. It was the summer after the war, and the
Ayreses still had most of their money then, were still big people in the district. The event was
an Empire Day féte: I stood with a line of other village children making a Boy Scout salute
while Mrs Ayres and the Colonel went past us, handing out commemorative medals;
afterwards we sat to tea with our parents at long tables on what I suppose was the south lawn.
Mrs Ayres would have been twenty-four or -five, her husband a few years older; their little
girl, Susan, would have been about six. They must have made a very handsome family, but my
memory of them is vague. I recall most vividly the house itself, which struck me as an absolute
mansion. I remember its lovely ageing details: the worn red brick, the cockled window glass,
the weathered sandstone edgings. They made it look blurred and slightly uncertain—like an

VII. In February 1922, Mahatma Gandhi decided to withdraw the Non-Cooperation Movement. He
felt the movement was turning violent in many places and satyagrahis needed to be properly
trained before they would be ready for mass struggles. Within the Congress, some leaders
were by now tired of mass struggles and wanted to participate in elections to the provincial
councils that had been set up by the Government of India Act of 1919. They felt that it was
important to oppose British policies within the councils, argue for reform and also
demonstrate that these councils were not truly democratic. C. R. Das and Motilal Nehru
formed the Swaraj Party within the Congress to argue for a return to council politics. But
younger leaders like Jawaharlal Nehru and Subhas Chandra Bose pressed for more radical
mass agitation and for full independence. In such a situation of internal debate and dissension
two factors again shaped Indian politics towards the late 1920s. The first was the effect of the
worldwide economic depression. Agricultural prices began to fall from 1926 and collapsed after
1930. As the demand for agricultural goods fell and exports declined, peasants found it
difficult to sell their harvests and pay their revenue. By 1930, the countryside was in turmoil.
Against this background the new Tory government in Britain constituted a Statutory
Commission under Sir John Simon. Set up in response to the nationalist movement, the
commission was to look into the functioning of the constitutional system in India and suggest
changes. The problem was that the commission did not have a single Indian member. They
were all British.
When the Simon Commission arrived in India in 1928, it was greeted with the slogan ‘Go back
Simon’. All parties, including the Congress and the Muslim League, participated in the
demonstrations. In an effort to win them over, the viceroy, Lord Irwin, announced in October
1929, a vague offer of ‘dominion status’ for India in an unspecified future, and a Round Table
Conference to discuss a future constitution. This did not satisfy the Congress leaders.

to safeguard India's energy supply lines through the strategically important Strait of Hormuz.
The initiative aims to ensure the safe passage of Indian-flagged and India-bound vessels
carrying essential energy cargo, including crude oil, liquefied petroleum gas (LPG), and
liquefied natural gas (LNG), through one of the world's busiest and most sensitive maritime
chokepoints.
The Strait of Hormuz is a critical global trade route, with nearly one-fifth of the world's
seaborne oil passing through it. Any disruption in this narrow waterway can significantly
affect international energy markets and India's energy security, as the country imports a
substantial share of its crude oil and natural gas from the Gulf region. Recognising these
risks, the Indian Navy has deployed more than five frontline warships to escort merchant
vessels, provide navigational assistance, and maintain a secure maritime environment.
Naval warships establish rendezvous points in the Gulf of Oman and accompany commercial
ships through safer waters after they clear the high-risk zone. The Navy has already
successfully escorted several vessels, including LPG carriers Pine Gas and Jag Vasant,
transporting nearly 92,000 tonnes of LPG, along with other crude oil and gas carriers. The
mission is being carried out in close coordination with the Ministry of Ports, Shipping and
Waterways, the Directorate General of Shipping, and other government agencies.
The deployment reflects India's evolving maritime strategy, where naval capabilities are
increasingly used to protect economic interests alongside national security. By ensuring

XIII. Environmental Safeguards in India: The EPA, 1986 and the EIA Framework
India's principal legislative instrument for environmental protection is the Environment
(Protection) Act, 1986 (EPA), which empowers the Central Government to take all necessary
measures for environmental quality improvement. The Act defines environmental pollution as
the presence of any solid, liquid, or gaseous substance at concentrations harmful to the
environment, and mandates that discharge of pollutants must not exceed prescribed
regulatory standards. Under the current EPA, contravention of Section 7 or Section 8 attracts
monetary penalty under Section 14A: 21 lakh to 215 lakh, with %50,000 per day for continuing
contravention. Notably, Section 19 of the EPA permits any person — not merely government
officials — to file a complaint before a court regarding violations after giving not less than 60
days’ notice to the Central Government or authorised authority.
Complementing the EPA is the Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA) framework,
operationalised through the EJA Notification, 2006. EIA is a systematic process of identifying,
predicting, and mitigating the environmental effects of proposed projects before they are
undertaken. Baseline environmental data must be sufficiently representative; reliance on only
one season may distort impact prediction. EIA applicability is determined by size, capacity,
area, location, sectoral, or schedule-based thresholds, not merely investment value. Some
projects may remain outside full EIA scrutiny because of these thresholds.
The EIA process requires the project proponent to prepare an EIA report, often through
consultants. Reports are funded by project proponents themselves, creating concerns of conflict
of interest, selective reporting, and weak accountability despite the accreditation framework.

XIV. Witness Protection Scheme, 2018 and Section 398 of the Bharatiya Nagarik
Suraksha Sanhita, 2023
The Witness Protection Scheme, 2018 was introduced to address the critical gap in protecting
witnesses who face threats for deposing against powerful accused persons. Before this Scheme,
India addressed witness protection through scattered provisions such as Section 232 of the
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (which criminalises threats to witnesses), but these did not provide
physical protection, relocation, or identity change. Since policing and public order are State
subjects, consensus could not be reached on a uniform national law for many years. High-
profile cases exposed this gap and the urgent need for a structured mechanism.
The Scheme categorises threats into three levels. Category A covers threats to life of witness
or family and provides measures such as relocation, change of identity, and video conferencing
with concealed identity. Category B covers threats to reputation or property, and Category C
covers moderate threats such as harassment. A Threat Analysis Report (TAR) prepared by
senior police officials assesses the danger to a witness, following which the competent
authority may order appropriate protection measures based on the threat level. The Scheme is
curative and remedial — it addresses threats after they arise. In contrast, bail cancellation
under Section 483 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita is a preventive and supervisory
judicial remedy for breach of bail conditions. The two are complementary but not
interchangeable.

XVI. Search, Seizure, and Attachment: CrPC and BNSS Compared
The investigation of a criminal offence involves three critical pre-trial powers: search, seizure,
and attachment. Under the Code of Criminal Procedure (CrPC), Sections 93-103 govern
search procedures. A Magistrate may issue a search warrant where evidence is not otherwise
obtainable or where items are suspected to be stolen or used in a crime. Section 165 CrPC
permits a police officer to search without a warrant during investigation if delay would
prejudice the case. All searches must be conducted in the presence of independent witnesses
called panchas, and compliance with Section 100 CrPC requires at least two respectable
inhabitants of the locality, preparation of a panchnama, and provision of a copy of the seized
articles list to the occupant.
Regarding seizure, Section 102 CrPC empowers police to seize property suspected to be stolen
or connected to a crime, with a mandatory report to the Magistrate. Sections 451-452 CrPC
confer judicial authority to dispose of or return property during and after trial. Attachment
under Section 83 CrPC applies to property of proclaimed offenders declared under Section 82,
covering both movable and immovable property. Section 105 CrPC extends attachment to
properties linked to offences committed outside India.www.lptedtech.com
The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS), 2023, replaces CrPC with significant
modernisation. BNSS contains search-warrant/search-related provisions in Sections 96-105
and separately provides for search by police officer during investigation under Section 185,
introducing electronic records and gender-sensitive procedures for searches involving women.
Section 106 BNSS corresponds broadly to police power to seize certain property. Section 105
BNSS introduces audio-video recording of search and seizure. Section 107 BNSS deals with
attachment, forfeiture, or restoration of property derived from criminal activity. Sections 87—
88 BNSS address attachment of proclaimed offenders' property, enabling digital notice
issuance and faster recovery proceedings.

XX. In an interesting turn of events, the breakaway faction of the All India Trinamool Congress
(AITMC) in the Lok Sabha announced merger with Nationalist Citizens Party of India (NCPD),
a regional party. The faction, with 20 MPs, has sought to invoke the merger exception under
the Tenth Schedule on the grounds that it has the support of two-thirds of AITMC’s legislature
party in Lok Sabha. While this may appear to be just another episode of political realignment,
it raises a deeper question about the working of the anti-defection law: Does the Tenth
Schedule permit two-thirds of a legislature party to effectively merge a political party with
another political party? The answer to this question goes to the heart of the merger exception,
a provision that was designed to safeguard genuine mergers between political parties. The
Tenth Schedule was enacted in 1985 to curb the politics of floor crossing among elected
legislators. It provides for disqualification of legislators who voluntarily give up membership of
their political party or defy its directions in the House. Yet, the law has often operated less as
a deterrent to defections and more as a framework within which they are meticulously
planned. Much of this can be attributed to the exceptions inherent in the law itself. The Tenth
Schedule never provided for an absolute prohibition on defections. Instead, the law exempted
disqualifications in cases of a “split” in a political party and “merger” of political parties. In
2004 the split exemption was omitted due to its excessive misuse while the merger exemption
continued to survive. Over the years, the merger exception has emerged as the principal route
for group defections to seek constitutional legitimacy in India. Housed within Paragraph 4 and
divided across two sub-paragraphs, the merger exception requires two conditions to be
fulfilled: first, an original political party must merge with another political party, and second,
a minimum of two-thirds of the members of the legislature party must consent to the merger.
Only when these two conditions are met, in this exact sequence, can a group of elected
legislators claim exemption from disqualification on grounds of merger. However, in practice,
the interpretation of Paragraph 4 has strayed from its original design, focusing primarily on
the second condition alone. This has led to an approach where the numerical majority of two-
thirds of the legislature party has been deemed to be sufficient condition to claim a merger,
regardless of the merger of the original political party with another party.
